lectures.framing: From a 2021-22 Foundations of Medicine summative note set, week 9. Gathers 4 of its sections, in the order they were written.

blocks.html:
• Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS): form a group of clonal hematopoietic stem cell malignancies characterized by ineffective hematopoiesis in one or more cell lineages, associated peripheral cytopenias, and risk of transformation to AML
  • 3-4 per 100,000; much more common in elderly patients (1 in 1000); median age = 65-70 years
  • Etiology: idiopathic or secondary to toxic exposures (chemotherapy, radiation, environmental toxins), may be associated with an underlying hereditary disorder or acquired mutations
  • Clinical presentation: anemia (80% at diagnosis, usually normocytic or macrocytic); neutropenia (40% at diagnosis), thrombocytopenia (30% at diagnosis), progression in AML
  • Ix: CBC (penias), ferritin (iron overload), BM aspirate/biopsy, flow cytometry, cytogenetics
  • International Prognostic Scoring System (IPSS): score is based on the number of blasts in the BM, chromosomal abnormalities, and number of cell lines involved
  • Lower-risk management: improve QoL, transfusions (< 70 gm/L), manage iron overload, growth factor support (EPO, G-CSF)
  • Higher-risk management: alter course of disease/slow progression; transfusions (< 70 gm/L), hypomethylating agents (azacytidine, decitabine), high dose chemotherapy, hematopoietic stem cell transplant
  • MDS with del(5q) occurs in < 10% of all MDS → macrocytic anemia, thrombocytosis; treat with lenalidomide (Revlimid)

• 20 mg of iron is recycled every day to make new RBCs – absorb and lose 1-2 mg/day
  • Molecular iron is not soluble and free ionic iron is toxic (bound to transferrin when transported in the blood)
  • Iron is the centerpiece in the heme molecule; malfunctioning of enzymes in heme biosynthesis can lead to porphyria
  • Ferritin: an iron storage protein composed of 24 identical protein subunits that form a hollow shell; can pack 4500 iron ions
  • Heme iron is bound to heme and taken up by heme carrier proteins (HCP); transported out by ferroportin and hephaestin Hepcidin can block ferroportin with iron concentrations are too high
  • Non-heme iron (Fe3+) is converted to Fe2+ by duodenal cytochrome B with the help of ascorbic acid, and then taken up by divalent metal transporter

lectures.title: Hemostasis
lectures.framing: From a 2021-22 Foundations of Medicine summative note set, week 10. Gathers 4 of its sections, in the order they were written.

blocks.html:
• Bleeding: to emit or lose blood
  • Hemostasis: a complex process in which multiple components of the blood clotting system are activated in response to vessel injury to control bleeding
  • 1. Primary hemostasis = vasoconstriction and platelet plug formation Triggered by injury to the vessel wall, exposing subendothelial collagen
  • Vasoconstriction: occurs at the site of injury to reduce blood flow – reflex neurogenic mechanisms
  • Adhesion: von Willebrand factor (vWF) adheres platelets to exposed subendothelial collagen via the platelet receptor glycoprotein Ib/IX (GPIb/IX); platelets also adhere directly to collagen via other receptors
  • Aggregation: platelets aggregate with each other with the help of fibrinogen that binds to activated glycoprotein IIb/IIIa (GPIIb/IIIa), forming a platelet plug Contraction: activation of platelet leads to shape change (discoid → spheroid); secretion of platelet granular content,
  • influx of calcium; platelet plug provides negatively charged phospholipid surface for coagulation factor assembly
  • Platelets → arachidonic acid – cyclooxygenase → endoperoxides – thromboxane synthase → thromboxane A2
  • 2. Secondary hemostasis = activation of coagulation factors and generation of thrombin/fibrin Initiation phase
  • Tissue factor (TF) is released from injured tissue cells, endothelial cells, and monocytes
  • TF and Factor VIIa form the TF/Factor VIIa complex
  • TF/Factor VIIa activates a small amount of Factor IX and X to generate a small amount of thrombin Factor XII (and other “contact” factors) play a minor role in the activation of Factor XI
  • Amplification phase
  • Thrombin activates Factor V to Va, Factor VIII to VIIIa and activates more platelets
  • Thrombin also activates FXI to FXIa
  • Propagation phase Additional Factor Xa is produced when TF/Factor VIIa complex activates Factor IX; the resultant Factor IXa
  • along with Factor VIIIa forms the tenase complex which then converts more Factor X to Xa
  • Factor Xa and Va along with calcium and a phospholipid (PL) surface (activated platelets) form the prothrombinase complex which converts prothrombin (Factor II) to large amounts of thrombin (Factor IIa)
target the generation of TF-VIIa and Xa
(Protein C and Protein S will target FV and VIII)
(antithrombin can bind to FIX, X and XI)

• 3. Fibrin clot formation and stabilization Thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin monomers which polymerize to form a soluble clot
  • Thrombin activates Factor XIII which cross-links the fibrin monomers and stabilizes the clot
  • 4. Inhibition of coagulation = inhibition of thrombin generation and fibrin clot breakdown (fibrinolysis) Tissue plasminogen activator (t-PA) converts plasminogen to plasmin – breaks down cross-linked fibrin to D-dimers
  • Thrombin activatable fibrinolysis inhibitor (TAFI) inhibits the formation of plasmin and suppresses fibrinolysis
  • Anti-plasmin and plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1) inhibit plasmin and t-PA

• Evaluating Coagulation in the Lab

  • Activated factors are indicated with an “a”

blocks.html:
• To assess coagulation “in vitro,” the laboratory measures the time taken to form a clot
  • Blood is collected into a blue top tube containing sodium citrate anticoagulant (which chelates calcium) to prevent blood clotting in the tube during transport
  • Plasma is separated from the platelets (phospholipid source) by centrifugation

• Prothrombin time (PT): used to assess deficiencies or inhibitors of the extrinsic pathway factors and common pathway factors
  • PT reagent (0.1 mL thromboplastin + phospholipids + calcium chloride) + plasma (0.05 mL); incubate at 37°C
  • Normal = 9-15 seconds → can be normal in mild factor deficiencies
  • International normalized ratio (INR): developed to standardize the PT to allow for monitoring of oral vitamin K antagonist therapy across different labs; PT in seconds is used to calculate the INR Normal = 0.9-1.1
  • Activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT): used to assess deficiencies or inhibitors of the intrinsic pathway factors and common pathway factors APTT reagent (0.1 mL contact activator + phospholipids) + plasma (0.1 mL) + CaCI2 (0.1 mL); incubate at 37°C
  • No tissue factor
  • Normal = 25-35 seconds → can be normal in mild factor deficiencies
  • Thrombin time (TT): used to assess deficiencies or dysfunction of fibrinogen or the presence of an inhibitor of thrombin Thrombin reagent (0.1 mL) + diluted plasma (0.2 mL); incubate at 37°C
  • Time in seconds is inversely proportional to fibrinogen activity – obtained from a standard calibration curve
  • Longer clotting time = lower concentration of fibrinogen in the sample
  • Fibrinogen assay: assesses fibrinogen activity
  • Hypofibrinogenemia: loss of fibrinogen (bleeding), consumption (hyperfibrinolysis after traumatic injury, DIC), decreased production (severe liver disease), congenital, dysfibrinogenemia (abnormal fibrinogen) Fibrinogen is an acute phase reactant and may be non-specifically elevated with acute or chronic inflammation
  • D-dimer tests: qualitative (positive or negative), quantitative (Enzyme Linked Immunosorbent Assay or Latex Immunoassay which use a monoclonal antibody to various epitopes of D-dimer) D-dimers: breakdown products generated by the action of plasmin on cross-linked fibrin
  • Negative D-dimer – used to rule out VTE
  • Elevated D-dimer – not specific to thrombosis; may be associated with other non-specific diseases or inflammatory states (recent surgery/trauma, cancer, acute/chronic infectious/inflammatory diseases, DIC, elderly, pregnancy)
  • Anti-Xa assay: used to measure the anticoagulant activity of an anticoagulant that inhibits clotting Factor Xa such as heparin, LMWH, fondaparinux or direct Xa inhibitors (rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban)
  • 50:50 mixing study: combine 1 part patient plasma with 1 part normal plasma to differentiate a factor deficiency or inhibitor
  • Correction = factor deficiency; does not correct = inhibitor; partial correction = multiple factor deficiencies or inhibitor
  • Well’s Criteria for DVT: active cancer; paralysis, paresis, or recent immobilization of lower extremities; recently bedridden > 3 days or major surgery within 4 weeks; localized tenderness along the distribution of the deep venous system; entire leg swollen; calf swelling 3 cm over the other side (measured 10 cm below tibial tuberosity); pitting edema confined to symptomatic leg; collateral superficial veins; no alternative diagnosis; previous history of DVT

  • 5. Put it all together for management

blocks.html:
• Radiation therapy: the use of ionizing radiation for the treatment of tumours
  • Damages the DNA of cells and destroys their ability to reproduce – both normal and cancer cells affected
  • All tissues have a tolerance level/maximum dose beyond which irreparable damage may occur (spinal cord, bowel, kidney, and lungs are often limiting)
  • Tumour directed radiation is delivered to the body either externally or internally

rows:
Uses x-ray (photon) or electron beams
10-15 minutes, 5 days/week for 1-10 weeks
Painless; most significant side effects occur near the end of the treatment course
Slight risk that radiation may cause a secondary cancer many years after treatment

Uses decaying radioactive isotopes placed in proximity to the tumour – gynecological and GU tumours
Low dose rate (LDR) permanent implants = radiation delivered over days to months
High dose rate (HDR) temporary implants = radiation delivered over minutes
Modern brachytherapy = ultra-precision; minimally invasive 3D image guided radiation implants, prostate/gynecologic tumours
Maximize the therapeutic ratio by sparing normal uninvolved tissues from high doses of radiation

Specialized form of highly focused external beam radiation (1 mm of accuracy) applying extremely high radiation doses
1-5 treatments using advanced treatment platforms
E.g., Gammaknife, Cyberknife, Trubeam

blocks.html:
• Fractionation: dividing the total dose into small daily fractions over several weeks
  • Takes advantage of differential repair abilities of normal and malignant tissues
  • Cancer cells (redistribution, reoxygenation) do not repair as effectively as normal cells (repair, repopulation)
  • Cells are most susceptible to DNA damage when they are in their mitotic cycle and their DNA is exposed (G2-M) Fast growing tumours are more radiosensitive and quicker to respond than slow growing tumours
  • Four Rs of Radiobiology
  • Repair of sublethal damage to cells between fractions caused by radiation
  • Repopulation or regrowth of cells between fractions
  • Redistribution of cells into radiosensitive phases of cell cycle
  • Reoxygenation of hypoxic cells to make them more sensitive to radiation

• 1. To cure cancer – destroy tumours that have not spread; kill residual microscopic disease after surgery/chemotherapy (adjuvant) Common sites: breast, prostate, lung, colorectal, pancreas, esophagus, head/neck, brain, skin, gynecologic, lymphomas,

  • 2. To reduce or palliate symptoms – shrink tumours affecting QoL (alleviate pain or neurological symptoms)
  • Other palliative uses: spinal cord compression, vascular compression (superior vena cava syndrome), bronchial obstruction, bleeding from GI or gynecologic tumours, esophageal obstruction

• EBM = patient values + clinical expertise + best research evidence
  • Descriptive research: correlational, qualitative study interview, case studies/reports
  • Analytical research: observational (cohort, case-control, cross-sectional), experimental (RCT, non-RCT, community trial)
  • Equipoise: an ethical concept in the design and conduct of clinical trials
  • 1. There is no evidence to suggest that any treatment or therapy in the trial is better than another
  • 2. There is no evidence to suggest that there is any therapy external to the trial that is better than the treatments being evaluated in the trial
  • Chance = random error; bias = systematic error
  • Methods to minimize bias: RCTs, double blind (masked), analysis (intention to treat)
  • Confounding: an association between two variables of interest (exposure and an outcome) that appears to be direct and causal, but in fact exists because of an unconsidered variable(s) and thus leads to a spurious interpretation of their relationship
  • 1. Must be an extraneous risk factor for the disease – related to the outcome
  • 2. Must be associated with the exposure under study in the population
  • 3. Must not be in the casual pathway between the exposure and disease
  • To have a fair and unbiased evaluation of randomized treatments, the outcome measures should ideally be evaluated in a blinded manner, where both the patient and the investigator responsible for evaluation of outcome are unaware of the treatment assignment (“double blinded”) Open label: all parties are aware of the treatment allocation
  • Single blind: either the patient or the clinician is unaware of the treatment allocation
  • Double blind: both the patient and the investigators are unaware of the treatment allocation
  • Triple blind: the patient, investigator, and analysts are unaware of the treatment allocation Unblinding: the disclosure of the allocation of treatment
  • Components of a study protocol: background and rationale for the study, study objective, overview of study design and graphical schema, patient eligibility and selection criteria, patient enrolment and randomization, treatment regimens, endpoints (primary, secondary), clinical evaluations, statistical considerations (sample size calculation, power statement, analysis plan), data collection methods, data safety and monitoring, patient plain language statement and informed consent form

blocks.html:
• Superiority trial: a trial with the primary objective of showing that the response to the investigational product is superior to a comparative agent
  • A new therapy is compared to placebo control, or a new therapy is expected to be better than an existing therapy
  • Non-inferiority trial: a trial with the primary objective of showing that the response to the investigational product is not clinically inferior to a comparative agent
  • A new experimental therapy might not be more efficacious than existing proven therapy, but it may offer other advantages – safety (less invasive/toxic), tolerability, convenience of administration/cost savings
  • Equivalence trial: a trial with the primary objective of showing that the response to two or more treatments differs by an amount which is clinically unimportant
  • This is usually demonstrated by showing that the true treatment difference is likely to lie between a lower and an upper equivalence margin of clinically acceptable differences
  • Intention-to-treat analysis: analysis of study groups according to which treatment they were assigned, and not according to which treatment they actually received in the end Everyone randomized in the trial is analyzed and all the follow-up information is included in the analysis, even if they
  • discontinued the assigned treatment
  • Considered as a de-facto standard for analysis and most journals and regulatory authorities insist on reporting this Almost always yields a more conservative estimate of the treatment effect and reflects real world setting
  • Per-protocol (PP) analysis: includes all patients who completed the full course of assigned treatment
  • Will usually yield a higher effect estimate of the treatment effect in this setting In general, the patients who did not comply with therapy and therefore omitted from a per-protocol analysis are those
  • who are unable to tolerate the treatment or are doing poorly
  • Non-inferiority margin/delta: the maximum clinically acceptable difference in efficacy between the new and existing therapy that one is willing to give up
  • Must be pre-specified
  • Is based on clinical judgement and statistical reasoning
  • Is how much the control arm efficacy can exceed the new treatment arm efficacy such that the new treatment can still be considered non-inferior to the control therapy A positive non-inferiority clinical trial implies that the experimental therapy is better than or no worse than the control
  • therapy by at least the value of the delta/non-inferiority margin
  • Primary endpoint: the main outcome measure that forms the basis for determination of the power of the study or the sample size required; commonly dichotomous (success or failure; null hypothesis vs. alternative hypothesis)
  • Composite endpoints: consist of 2 or more binary endpoints and may be the primary endpoint of a clinical trial Patients experiencing any of the events from the eligible set (the components) of endpoints are considered to have
  • experienced the composite endpoint of interest
  • All individual endpoints within composite endpoint are equally weighted To avoid the problem of introducing bias from competing risks, it is important that the composite endpoint consists of
  • the events of interest and “anything worse” such as death
  • p-value – usually < 0.05; consider the total study population and the number of events in each group
  • Confidence interval – usually 95%
  • One-sided test: investigators suspect a difference in response between two groups in one direction only; smaller sample size
  • Two-sided test: investigators are unsure of the direction of difference in response between two groups
  • Type I error (𝜶)= false positive rate; Type II error (𝜷) = false negative rate
  • Power: the probability of finding a difference between groups when a true treatment difference exists; power = 1 – 𝜷
  • Subgroup analysis: performed to examine whether treatment differences appear consistent across all types of patients or vary according to subgroups
